input.question: why is the permeability of free space such a "clean " number?
input.ground_truth: Because we defined the amp as > the constant current that will produce an attractive force of 2 × 10^(−7) newtons per metre of length between two straight, parallel conductors of infinite length and negligible circular cross section placed one metre apart in a vacuum and so we end up with a clean number for the permeability of free space and a messy number for number of electrons needed for a charge of one coulomb. We could have defined a coulomb as, say, the charge of 10^18 electrons, an amp as one of those coulombs per second, and then the permeability of free space would be the messy number instead.

Question: why is the permeability of free space such a "clean " number?

Okay! Imagine you have a little toy car and you want to drive it through a soft, squishy sponge. Some sponges are really easy to drive through (they’re "clean" and open), and some are hard and make it tough for the car to go through.

Now, imagine there’s a special sponge called "free space" that scientists use when they want to know how easy it is for things like light or electricity to move through nothing at all (that’s what "free space" means—there’s nothing there!).

The "permeability of free space" is a special number that tells us just how easy it is for these things to move through this empty space. The number is very "clean" and simple because empty space doesn’t have anything to block or change the way things move. It’s like the sponge is perfectly smooth and the same everywhere, so the number that describes it doesn’t get messy or complicated. That’s why it’s called a "clean" number!
